court: New York Court for the Correction of Errors
justification: The court affirms the landlord's unilateral election to treat a holdover tenant as bound by the original lease's terms, including the right to distrain for rent payable in advance, while denying the tenant any corresponding election to disclaim the tenancy. This protects the owner's contractual control over the letting relationship and his remedies for collecting rent on his own terms.
supporting_quote: The landlord has an election to treat him either as a trespasser, or as a tenant... The tenant has no such election as that which belongs to the landlord.

justification: The court rejected the tenant's claim that the landlord's continued occupation of a room (after boarding ceased) constituted an eviction suspending rent, holding instead that the landlord's payment for use and occupation removed any technical eviction and upheld the landlord's distress for rent. This affirms the owner's right to collect compensation for occupancy and rejects an expansion of tenant remedies against the owner.
supporting_quote: It was not an eviction in law, consequently there is no defense on that ground... his subsequent payment to them for the use and occupation thereof, took from the case the technical character of an eviction by a landlord.
holding: A landlord who boarded and lodged in a room of the house he had let to his tenants, by their permission and subordinate to their rights, was not thereby evicting them; his subsequent payment for use and occupation of the room after he ceased boarding removed any technical character of eviction, so the tenants' distress for rent was upheld.

justification: The court held there is no implied covenant that a leased dwelling is fit for habitation, and refused to let the tenant assert damages from an unhealthy condition (caused by a neighbor, without landlord fault) as a counter-claim against rent owed. This preserves the owner's freedom to let on his own terms without implied habitability obligations, rejecting an expansion of tenant rights against the owner.
supporting_quote: There is no implied covenant on the part of the landlord that premises let for a private residence, are fit for such purpose.
holding: There is no implied covenant that a house let for use as a private residence, even a furnished one, is fit for habitation; where noxious gases from a neighbor's stable made the leased dwelling unhealthy but neither landlord nor tenant knew of the condition and the landlord was not at fault, the tenant could not assert the resulting damages as a counter-claim to the landlord's action for rent.

justification: The Court of Appeals affirmed that no covenant of habitability is implied in a lease of a furnished dwelling, and that the tenant who examined the premises and continued to occupy remained liable for rent despite noxious odors from a neighboring stable. This keeps the burden of unfitness on the tenant (caveat emptor) and protects the owner from implied duties that would restrict his letting terms.
supporting_quote: The lessee of real property must run the risk of its condition, unless he has an express agreement on the part of the lessor in relation thereto.
holding: In an action for the last quarter's rent under a one-year lease of a furnished dwelling-house, the court held there was no implied covenant that the house was fit for habitation where noxious odors from a neighboring livery stable, unknown to either party when the lease was made and not originating on the demised premises, made the house unhealthy; the tenant, who had examined the premises and continued to occupy them, remained liable for the rent.

justification: The court squarely holds that a householder (here, a lessee-occupant) may admit boarders, lodgers, and roomers into the dwelling on whatever terms she chooses without losing the character of a private dwelling or committing an unlawful sublease. This directly recognizes and protects the occupant/owner's liberty to let space for compensation on her own terms.
supporting_quote: But certainly a householder may admit into his house, and on whatever condition he chooses, whomsoever he will, including boarders, lodgers and roomers; nor does his home thereby cease to be his private dwelling.
holding: A lessor sought to annul a lease and dispossess a tenant who had taken in boarders, lodgers, and roomers, on the ground the premises were rented only as a dwelling and the arrangement was an unconsented sublease. The court held a householder may admit into her house, on whatever condition she chooses, whomever she will, including boarders, lodgers and roomers, without her home ceasing to be a private dwelling, and further held that renting rooms to friends while the tenant retains overall superintendence of the premises is not a 'sublease' requiring the lessor's written consent.

justification: The court holds that a building with a pastor's family plus three paying female roomers does not qualify as a 'multiple dwelling,' because the roomers are not a separate 'family living independently,' and therefore the statutory lighting duty under the Multiple Dwelling Law does not attach. This shields the owner from a regulatory burden that would otherwise be triggered by letting rooms to lodgers, effectively protecting the owner's freedom to let a small number of rooms without incurring additional statutory duties.
supporting_quote: Upon the facts stated, the premises of the defendant do not come within the purview of the Multiple Dwelling Law.
holding: The court held that a church building housing the pastor's family together with three paying female roomers (who ate separately, cooked for by a matron) was not a "multiple dwelling" under the Multiple Dwelling Law, because the roomers did not constitute a separate "family" living independently. Consequently the statutory lighting-duty claim against the landlord failed.

justification: The court shields the owner, who let the building 'as is' to a tenant for use as a rooming house, from any duty to guests of sub-tenants once out of possession, applying the general rule that a landlord out of possession owes no duty for conditions existing when the tenant took occupancy. This protects the owner's freedom to let premises without an implied duty to guarantee habitability to subsequent occupants, consistent with an owner's right to let on the owner's own terms.
supporting_quote: The general rule is that the landlord who is entirely out of possession and control is not liable for bodily harm caused to the tenant and those upon the leased premises in the latter's right by reason of any dangerous condition existing when the tenant took possession.

court: Court of Appeal of Louisiana, Orleans
justification: The court reversed a judgment for the ousted tenant and dismissed her bad-faith claim, holding that the owner's later letting of two furnished rooms to two roomers (with the owner occupying the remainder) fell outside the federal definition of regulated 'controlled housing accommodations.' This recognizes an exemption preserving the owner's freedom to let on the owner's own terms without triggering rent-control restrictions, and rejects the tenant's attempt to expand recovery against the owner.
supporting_quote: the accommodations which Kemp rented after Mary Blanchard removed were rented furnished to not more than two paying tenants not members of the landlord's immediate family... the act had no application to these particular accommodations
holding: In a suit over a landlord's alleged bad-faith use of a rent-control eviction certificate, the court held that the landlord's later renting of two furnished rooms to two roomers was not evidence of bad faith, because such nonhousekeeping furnished accommodations let to no more than two non-family paying tenants (with the landlord occupying the remainder of the unit) fall outside the federal definition of regulated 'controlled housing accommodations.' The judgment for the ousted tenant was reversed and her suit dismissed.

court: Court of Civil Appeals of Texas, Waco
justification: The court expressly rejected any implied warranty of habitability or implied duty to repair arising from a residential lease absent an express agreement, holding that a tenant takes the premises as he finds them under the doctrine of caveat emptor. This directly affirms the owner's liberty to let a dwelling on the owner's own terms, free of judicially-imposed habitability or repair duties.
supporting_quote: The mere relation of landlord and tenant creates no obligation on the part of the landlord to repair or keep in repair the leased premises. The tenant takes the premises as he finds them.
holding: The court held that a residential landlord's oral month-to-month letting of an apartment carries no implied warranty of habitability or implied duty to repair absent an express agreement, applying the traditional caveat-emptor rule to leases in Texas.

justification: The court rejected the tenant's attempt to imply a covenant that leased premises were fit for a 'first class' boarding house beyond what was expressly stated in the lease, and affirmed judgment for the landlord owners on the unpaid rent where no fraud was proven. This protects the owner's freedom to let on the terms actually stated in the lease, refusing to expand implied obligations against the owner.
supporting_quote: Conceding that there is an implied covenant in the lease that the premises when let, were fit and suitable for occupation as boarding houses, such covenant cannot be so extended by implication as to cover first class, or any particular description of boarding houses not expressly designated in the lease.
holding: In an action for rent under leases of two houses hired to be operated as a boarding house, the court held that even if a covenant is implied that leased premises are fit for occupation as a boarding house, that implied covenant does not extend by implication to fitness for a 'first class' or any other particular description of boarding house not expressly stated in the lease, and affirmed judgment for the landlords where no fraud or misrepresentation as to nearby nuisances was proven.

justification: The court held that the statutory summary proceeding for nonpayment of rent applies equally to furnished lettings as to unfurnished ones, rejecting the tenant's narrow construction that would have stripped the owner of the summary remedy simply because furniture was included in the demise. This affirms and facilitates the owner's ability to let (including furnished units) and to enforce the letting through the owner's chosen statutory remedy.
supporting_quote: The remedy furnished by the statute extends to all of the cases just referred to. ... The landlord is entitled to judgment.
holding: In a summary proceeding to dispossess a tenant of a furnished house for nonpayment of rent, the court held that the statutory summary remedy applies to furnished lettings the same as to unfurnished ones. The tenant's argument that including furniture in the demise removed the case from the statute was rejected as an unwarranted narrow construction, and judgment was given for the landlord.

justification: The case upholds a landlord's statutory summary proceeding to recover possession from a tenant for failure to pay agreed rent, rejecting the tenant's attempt to escape the remedy because furniture was included in the letting. The ruling protects the owner's ability to enforce her lease terms and swiftly recover possession, affirming the owner's freedom to let (including furnished lettings) on her own terms.
supporting_quote: the fact that furniture was embraced in the lease of the realty did not defeat the summary remedy awarded by statute, as the furniture was a mere incident of the grant, and the landlord had judgment
holding: Summary proceedings to dispossess a tenant under the statute may be maintained against the occupant of a furnished house. Furniture included in the letting is a mere incident of the grant of the realty, so its inclusion does not defeat the landlord's statutory dispossess remedy or make the fixed rent apportionable.

court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
justification: The court reversed an injunction that had blocked a landlord's summary dispossession proceeding against a tenant of a furnished house, holding the statutory remedy fully applies regardless of furniture being included in the letting. This protects the owner's contractual right to let furnished premises at a gross rent and to use the full statutory remedy to recover possession, favoring the owner's control over the letting arrangement.
supporting_quote: The order appealed from should be reversed, with ten dollars costs and disbursements of the appeal, and the injunction dissolved.
holding: The court held that statutory summary proceedings for non-payment of rent apply to a lessee of a fully furnished house let at a gross rent, because the furniture is a mere incident to the letting and the rent, in law, issues out of the land only; the injunction restraining the landlord's summary proceedings was therefore reversed.

justification: The court held that a landlord's timely notice that any holdover would be month-to-month defeated the tenant's claim to an implied year-long renewal, allowing the landlord to reclaim possession without extended notice despite the tenant's rent payments and boarding-house business on the premises. This affirms the owner's right to dictate the terms of continued occupancy and to avoid an unwanted long-term tenancy being imposed against her wishes.
supporting_quote: if, at or before the expiration of the former lease, the tenant was informed that he would not be permitted... to occupy the rented premises otherwise than as a tenant from month to month, and not for a year, then no contract that he should occupy the property for a year could be implied
holding: A landlord's agent notified a holdover tenant, who leased the house to run a boarding-house business, before the lease term ended that any continued occupancy would be month-to-month only. The court held that this notice defeated any implied one-year renewal despite the tenant's continued rent payments, so the landlord could recover possession without further notice.

justification: The court rejected the tenant's claim of constructive eviction from vermin-infested rooms, holding that caveat emptor applies to leases just as to sales and that landlords owe no implied warranty of habitability absent fraud or express agreement, affirming judgment for the landlord for unpaid rent. This strongly favors the owner's freedom to let premises on an as-is basis without assuming habitability burdens imposed against his will.
supporting_quote: The landlord, in the absence of fraud or express condition, is not responsible for the presence of rats, mice, bugs or roaches about his premises.
holding: A tenant leased a suite of rooms in the plaintiff's apartment house, the 'Four Seasons,' for one year, then abandoned the premises after about six months, claiming the rooms were rendered untenantable by vermin (bedbugs, cockroaches, water bugs, ants). The court held the landlord owed no implied warranty of habitability absent fraud or an express condition, applying caveat emptor to the leasing of the rooms just as to a sale, and affirmed judgment for the landlord for the unpaid rent.

justification: The court held that letting furnished apartments to lodgers by the month did not forfeit the lease under a covenant against subletting, since an apartment occupant holds only a license to occupy designated rooms, and the lessor's long acceptance of rent with knowledge of the practice amounted to a license to operate the building as an apartment house. This directly protects an owner's freedom to let rooms to lodgers on the owner's own terms without incurring forfeiture.
supporting_quote: Letting rooms to lodgers is held not to be a breach of a covenant against under-letting.
holding: The court held that letting furnished apartments to lodgers by the month did not breach a lease covenant against under-letting or assigning, because an apartment occupant holds only a license-like right to occupy designated rooms rather than an estate carved out of the term. The lessor's acceptance of rent for a series of years with knowledge that the building was operated as an apartment house was construed as a license to use it that way, not a mere recurring waiver. The lessee therefore did not forfeit the lease by letting apartments to monthly lodgers.

cite: Franklin v. Brown, 27 N.Y. St. Rep. 955
justification: The court refused to imply any covenant of habitability in a furnished-house lease, holding the tenant liable for rent despite noxious odors from a neighboring stable, because the landlord neither caused nor controlled the condition. This rejects an expansion of tenant/occupant rights against the owner and instead protects the owner's freedom to let property on the owner's own terms without added habitability obligations, consistent with favorable polarity.
supporting_quote: There is no implied covenant in a lease of a furnished house for a year which will justify a tenant in refusing to pay rent because of noxious gases and odors which come from adjoining premises used as a livery stable.
holding: The Court of Appeals held that a one-year lease of a furnished dwelling house carries no implied covenant that the premises are fit for habitation, so a tenant could not withhold rent because noxious odors migrated in from a neighboring livery stable that neither the landlord nor the tenant knew of and that the landlord did not cause.

justification: The court held that no covenant of habitability is implied in a lease of an unfurnished dwelling absent an express warranty or the lessor's fraudulent concealment, so the tenant remained liable for rent despite unsanitary plumbing. By declining to impose habitability duties on the owner absent fraud, the decision preserves the owner's liberty to let the dwelling on the terms actually contracted for.
supporting_quote: the law does not imply a covenant on the part of the lessor that the dwelling is without inherent defects rendering it unfit for a residence
holding: A householder leased her whole unfurnished dwelling for a one-year term with no covenant as to condition or repair; the court held that no covenant of habitability is implied in such a lease absent an express warranty or fraudulent concealment by the lessor, so the tenant remained liable for rent after abandoning the house for insanitary plumbing.

justification: The court upheld a married woman's lease of her boarding house and furniture and enforced the tenant's obligation to pay rent for the full term, rejecting the tenant's eviction defense based on the lessor's occasional bad language toward other boarders while she herself boarded in the house. This affirms the owner's capacity to let (including as a married woman) and protects her right to collect rent under the lease on her own terms, without expanding tenant/occupant rights against her.
supporting_quote: no amount of bad talk between Mrs. Ewing and the tenants there could amount to such an eviction as the law contemplates
holding: The Superior Court affirmed judgment for a landlady who had leased her boarding house and furniture to a tenant for a year, holding the lease properly admitted in evidence despite her coverture, that the tenant could not dispute the lessor's title because she took possession under it without eviction by any paramount title, and that the lessor's occasional bad language toward other boarders while herself boarding in the house did not as a matter of law amount to an eviction excusing the rent.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
justification: The court held that, absent an express covenant restricting the building exclusively to leased apartments, the landlord of an 'Apartment Hotel' could also let other rooms to transient day guests without breaching the term tenant's lease or effecting a constructive eviction. This squarely recognizes and protects the owner's liberty to let rooms in the building on the owner's own terms.
supporting_quote: in the absence of an express covenant that no portion of the building would be rented otherwise than in apartments as aforesaid, that plaintiff was guilty of a breach of any contract with defendant when it undertook to lease rooms in the building to transient tenants
holding: Absent an express covenant restricting an 'Apartment Hotel' exclusively to leased apartments, the landlord may also lease other rooms in the building to transient guests by the day; doing so does not breach the term tenant's lease or constitute a constructive eviction.

court: Court of Civil Appeals of Texas, El Paso
justification: The court held that a room let by a hotel on a day-to-day basis is not a wartime 'housing accommodation' subject to rent-control tenancy protections, and that an innkeeper may eject such an occupant on reasonable notice without resort to judicial eviction process. This directly protects the owner's/innkeeper's liberty to let short-term on the owner's own terms, free of statutory tenancy protections and legal-process requirements that would otherwise burden repossession.
supporting_quote: a hotel room let on a day basis was not a "housing accommodation."
holding: A hotel guest who had occupied a room on a day-to-day (and usually weekly) basis for about sixteen months was put out and his belongings moved to the lobby without judicial process; the court held the eviction lawful because a room let by a hotel from day to day is not a wartime 'housing accommodation' and an innkeeper may eject a guest on reasonable notice without resort to legal process. Finding no violation of a legal right, the court reversed the plaintiff's judgment and rendered judgment for the hotel proprietor.

justification: The court's dispositive reasoning rests on Multiple Dwelling Law §248(1), which it construes as affirmatively permitting a family/occupant to let rooms within an apartment to up to four boarders, roomers or lodgers as a lawful use, not a violation warranting eviction. This directly recognizes and protects the liberty to let rooms for compensation on the letting party's own terms, rather than expanding occupant rights against that liberty.
supporting_quote: This section shall not be construed to prohibit the letting by a family of one or more rooms within their apartment to not more than a total of four boarders, roomers or lodgers.
holding: In dispossess proceedings alleging illegal single-room occupancy under Multiple Dwelling Law §§248 and 302, the court held the landlord failed to prove a violation, noting that section 248(1) expressly permits a family to let rooms within its apartment to up to four boarders, roomers or lodgers without illegality.

court: Nassau County District Court, First District
justification: The court affirmed that a co-owner holding property as a tenant by the entirety may lease her interest to another without her co-tenant's consent, and that the non-consenting co-tenant (himself in possession) has no right to evict the lessee — only a right to share occupancy. This squarely recognizes the owner's liberty to let property on her own terms even over a co-owner's objection, so the prior favorable holding stands.
supporting_quote: The wife has the absolute right to lease her interest to respondent (her sister). Since petitioner currently resides at the premises, there is no relief available to petitioner in this summary proceeding.
holding: Where property is held by spouses as tenants by the entirety, one tenant may lease her interest to another without the other's consent; the non-consenting co-tenant who is himself already in possession has no exclusive right against the lessee and the eviction proceeding must be dismissed.

court: Supreme Court, General Term, Fifth Department
justification: This is a narrow evidentiary ruling reversing exclusion of proof that the holdover occupant paid rent to a joint owner rather than accepting the plaintiff's proposed renewal terms, rebutting the presumption of an implied contract at the higher rate. The case turns on ordinary landlord-tenant contract formation and does not impose any regulatory restriction on letting or expand occupant rights against an owner, so the owner's freedom to let for compensation on agreed terms is unaffected and the original favorable classification stands.
supporting_quote: it was to rebut that presumption, and account for the continued occupancy of the defendant on another theory than that of the acceptance of the plaintiff's proposition, that the evidence in question was offered

court: New York Supreme Court, Kings Trial Term
justification: The court upheld the landlord's right to summarily dispossess tenants and remove a sub-occupant (desk-hirer) who paid for space by the month, holding he had no independent estate because his position was 'no better than that of one with a room in a boarding or lodging house.' This protects the owner/head-tenant's freedom to let space for compensation without the letting creating an estate that could hamper lawful recovery of possession.
supporting_quote: His position was no better than that of one with a room in a boarding or lodging house. He had to go out with them.
holding: A person who hires desk room within a single undivided office from the tenants of that room has no independent tenancy or estate in the realty; when the landlord lawfully dispossesses the tenants without joining the desk-hirer, he cannot recover damages for being removed along with them, because his occupancy was legally no different from that of a person renting a room in a boarding or lodging house.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
justification: The case treats the plaintiff's business of letting furnished rooms for compensation as an ordinary, lawful enterprise and enforces the landlord's written lease terms (including the security deposit arrangement) strictly against the tenant's attempt to escape her own bill of sale. No restriction is placed on letting, and the owner's contractual terms controlling the tenancy are upheld over the tenant's claim.
supporting_quote: The plaintiff occupied the house for carrying on the business of renting furnished rooms.
holding: A tenant who leased a house to operate the business of renting furnished rooms sold that business, together with the lease and its security deposit, by an unambiguous bill of sale; the court held she could not avoid the transfer of her interest in the security by claiming she could not read English, absent any showing of fraud or mistake.

justification: The court squarely protected the owner's liberty to let rooms in its building to transient guests on its own terms, rejecting the tenant's claim that doing so breached quiet enjoyment or constituted eviction, absent an express restrictive covenant in the written lease. This directly affirms the owner's freedom to let as it sees fit against an attempt to imply a restriction.
supporting_quote: it by no means follows... that plaintiff was guilty of a breach of any contract with defendant when it undertook to lease rooms in the building to transient tenants
holding: The Appellate Term reversed a judgment for a tenant who had leased an apartment-hotel suite for a year and stopped paying rent after learning the hotel also let rooms to transient guests. The court held that letting some rooms to transients did not breach any covenant of quiet enjoyment absent an express restriction in the written lease confining the building to non-transient apartment use.

cite: Wilkes-Barre Realty Co. v. Levy, 114 N.Y.S. 713
justification: The court protected the landlord's ability to let a ground-floor unit for a 'table boarders' business without exposing itself to constructive-eviction liability to other tenants, holding that eviction cannot be predicated on conduct not committed, encouraged, or connived at by the landlord. This shields the owner's freedom to let space for a boarding arrangement from being used to restrict its rights elsewhere in the building.
supporting_quote: an eviction cannot be predicated of acts or conduct, however wrongful or distressing, unless committed, encouraged, or connived at by the landlord
holding: An apartment tenant was not constructively evicted by noise and odors from a ground-floor occupant's table-boarding arrangement, because the landlord neither caused, authorized, nor knew of the disturbance. Constructive eviction cannot rest on acts or conduct, however wrongful or distressing, unless committed, encouraged, or connived at by the landlord.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
justification: The court refuses to expand the constructive-eviction doctrine to conditions (dead rats causing a stench) that arose without any act or omission of the landlord, holding the tenant remains bound to pay rent despite the hardship absent landlord fault or a controlling statute. This upholds the owner's right to enforce the lease on his own terms and declines to impose an implied habitability-style duty beyond what the landlord caused, which favors the owner's position.
supporting_quote: In the absence of statute a constructive eviction can take place only where the tenant is deprived of his enjoyment of the demised premises by the act or omission of the landlord... the tenant must continue to bear his obligation to pay rent, however great the hardship, unless he has been relieved of this obligation by statute.

justification: The court enforces the owner's right to collect rent under a month-to-month letting notwithstanding the tenant's claim that the landlord breached a repair covenant, holding that continued use and occupancy without proof of unfitness or a counterclaim for damages does not excuse rent. This upholds the owner's ability to enforce his letting terms and recover the agreed compensation, favoring the owner's position rather than expanding tenant rights against him.
supporting_quote: appellee was liable for the rent for the three months' admitted use and occupancy of the building
holding: The court held that a landlord's breach of a covenant to repair a leaking roof did not excuse the tenant's rent obligation for months he continued to use and occupy the building as a grocery store and rooming house, absent proof the leaks rendered the building unfit for use or any counterclaim for offsetting damages.

court: New York Court of Special Sessions
justification: The court reversed all three convictions by finding the arrangement was primarily a personal-services (nursing) contract, not a landlord-tenant relationship, so rent regulation's tenant-removal and registration protections never attached; the owner could terminate the arrangement at will and regain her rooms. This vindicates the owner's freedom to structure and end an occupancy arrangement on her own terms free of tenant-protective regulation.
supporting_quote: Considered as a contract for personal services, appellant could terminate it at will.
holding: The court found the arrangement between a practical nurse occupying part of her own two-family house and an invalid boarder's family was primarily a contract for nursing services with incidental use of rooms, not a landlord-tenant relationship subject to rent regulation, and reversed the appellant's convictions for rent overcharge, unlawful removal, and failure to register.

justification: The court held the landlord committed no unlawful 'evasion' by registering and renting rooms as sleeping rooms with kitchen privileges rather than as a single apartment, even though this permitted a higher rent ceiling; she was legally entitled to structure the letting either way and to collect the higher registered rate. This directly affirms the owner's liberty to configure and price her letting on her own terms within the bounds of lawful registration.
supporting_quote: In renting her quarters to these plaintiffs defendant performed no wrongful, fraudulent or illegal act. Her actions amounted only to the legally permitted avoidance of an alternate and a lower rental ceiling.
holding: A householder who registered part of her apartment as two sleeping rooms with kitchen privileges under OPA rent regulations, rather than as a single apartment, did not thereby commit an unlawful 'evasion' of the lower apartment rent ceiling; she was entitled to rent the space either way, and the higher ceiling for the sleeping-room registration governed.

cite: Branic International Realty Corp. v. Pitt, 30 Misc. 3d 29 (N.Y. 2010)
court: Supreme Court, Appellate Term, First Department
justification: The Appellate Term reversed the lower court and granted the property owner summary judgment for possession, holding that because a city agency (not the owner) had placed and paid for the occupant, no landlord-tenant relationship arose and the occupant was merely a licensee with no permanent-tenant protections. This affirms the owner's right to recover the unit and to let it under an arrangement of its own choosing without being bound by rent-stabilization tenancy protections.
supporting_quote: Since respondent's license was revoked and he has no right to continued possession (see RPAPL 713 [7]), petitioner's cross motion for summary judgment on its claim for possession should have been granted.
holding: The Appellate Term reversed the Civil Court and held that because a city agency (HRA), not respondent, had placed respondent in petitioner's SRO hotel room and paid the room charge directly to petitioner, no express or implied landlord-tenant relationship arose; respondent was merely a licensee of HRA whose license had been revoked, not a rent-stabilized 'permanent tenant,' and petitioner was granted summary judgment on its claim for possession.
